# 4. Simulation Study

## 4.1 Overview

Three simulation studies were conducted to evaluate the statistical
properties of `measuredES`. Study 1 examined the bias and root mean
square error (RMSE) of the corrected and uncorrected effect-size
estimators. Study 2 examined the coverage probability and width of
the Hunter–Schmidt and Bonett confidence intervals, with a focused
sub-study adding the BCa bootstrap (Section 4.5). Study 3 examined
the consequences of reliability heterogeneity in a meta-analytic
context. All simulations were implemented in R (version 4.5.3) using
the `parallel` package for multi-core execution. Each study used
`set.seed(2026)` for reproducibility. Full simulation code is
available at https://github.com/gulince/measuredES.

## 4.2 Data-Generation Model

### 4.2.1 Classical Test Theory Parameterization

Data were generated under the standard CTT model $X = T + E$.
True scores were drawn from either a standard normal distribution
($T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$) or a standardized chi-squared
distribution with four degrees of freedom to represent a positively
skewed condition (skewness $\approx 1.41$). For the treatment group,
the true-score mean was shifted by $\delta$ (the population effect
size), so that $T_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\delta, 1)$.

Error variance was set to reproduce the target reliability exactly:

$$\sigma^2_E = \frac{1 - \rho_{xx}}{\rho_{xx}},$$

which ensures $\text{Var}(X) = 1/\rho_{xx}$ and
$\text{Var}(T)/\text{Var}(X) = \rho_{xx}$. Under this
parameterization, $d_{\text{obs}}$ estimates $\delta \sqrt{\rho_{xx}}$
and the corrected $\hat{\delta}$ estimates $\delta$, up to the usual
small-sample bias of $d$ [@hedges1981].

### 4.2.2 Reliability Estimation Conditions

Two reliability conditions were crossed with all other factors.
In the *known* condition, the population $\rho_{xx}$ was supplied
directly to the correction formula. In the *estimated* condition,
$\rho_{xx}$ was estimated from a simulated $k = 10$ item test using
Cronbach's $\alpha$ computed from item responses generated under the
tau-equivalent model. The Spearman–Brown formula was used to
determine per-item reliability such that the $k$-item composite
achieved the target $\rho_{xx}$. We used $\alpha$ because it equals
the reliability under tau-equivalence, the model that generated the
items; with real, typically congeneric data, $\alpha$ underestimates
$\rho_{xx}$ and $\omega$-type coefficients are preferable
[@mcneish2018]. The package is agnostic on this point: any
reliability estimate enters through the same `rxx` argument.

## 4.3 Study 1 and Study 2 Design

A fully crossed factorial design with the following factors was used:

- **Population effect size** ($\delta$): 0.20, 0.50, 0.80
  (small, medium, large; @cohen1988)
- **Sample size per group** ($n$): 30, 60, 120, 240
- **Reliability** ($\rho_{xx}$): 0.60, 0.75, 0.85, 0.95
- **Reliability condition**: known vs. estimated
- **Score distribution**: normal vs. skewed

This yielded $3 \times 4 \times 4 \times 2 \times 2 = 192$ conditions.
Each condition was replicated $R = 5{,}000$ times, for a total of
960,000 simulated experiments.

The factor levels were chosen to span realistic research conditions
rather than to stress-test extremes. The reliability values
0.60--0.95 cover the range typically documented for published
psychological measures in reliability generalization studies
[e.g., @vacha1998]; group sizes of 30--240 run from small laboratory
experiments to well-powered field studies; and the 10-item test used
in the estimated-reliability condition matches the length of many
brief self-report scales.

### 4.3.1 Performance Criteria

**Study 1 (point estimation):**

- *Bias*: $\hat{\delta} - \delta$
- *Relative bias* (%): $100 \times (\hat{\delta} - \delta) / \delta$
- *RMSE*: $\sqrt{E[(\hat{\delta} - \delta)^2]}$

**Study 2 (confidence intervals):**

- *Coverage probability*: proportion of intervals containing $\delta$
  (nominal: 0.95)
- *Mean CI width*
- *Asymmetric miss rates*: proportion of intervals falling entirely
  above or below $\delta$

Following the reporting recommendations of @morris2019, we note the
Monte Carlo uncertainty of these estimates. With $R = 5{,}000$, the
Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage estimate near the nominal
0.95 is $\sqrt{0.95 \times 0.05 / 5000} \approx 0.003$, and the
Monte Carlo standard error of the bias estimates stays below 0.005
in all conditions. All 5,000 replications completed successfully in
every condition.

## 4.4 Study 3 Design

Study 3 examined the meta-analytic consequences of ignoring
reliability differences across studies. A random-effects model was
simulated with the following factors:

- **Number of studies** ($k$): 5, 10, 20
- **Mean population effect** ($\delta_{\mu}$): 0.30, 0.50
- **Reliability pattern**:
  - *Homogeneous*: $\rho_{xx} = 0.85$ for all studies
  - *Heterogeneous*: $\rho_{xx} \sim \text{Beta}(8, 4)$
    (mean $\approx 0.67$, SD $\approx 0.13$), a distribution whose
    center and spread reflect the between-study variation in score
    reliability documented in reliability generalization work
    [e.g., @vacha1998]

This yielded $3 \times 2 \times 2 = 12$ conditions, each replicated
$R = 1{,}000$ times. For each replication, $k$ primary studies were
generated with sample sizes drawn uniformly from
$\{40, 60, 100, 150, 250\}$. True effect sizes varied across studies
as $\delta_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\delta_{\mu}, 0.10)$ to reflect
realistic between-study heterogeneity. Random-effects meta-analysis
was conducted using the `metafor` package [@viechtbauer2010] with
restricted maximum likelihood (REML) estimation, applied separately
to uncorrected and corrected effect sizes. Performance was evaluated
using bias, RMSE, and coverage probability of the 95% confidence
interval for the pooled estimate. With $R = 1{,}000$, the Monte
Carlo standard error of a coverage estimate near 0.95 is
approximately 0.007. REML estimation failed to converge in at most
three replications per condition (completion rate $\geq$ 99.7%);
non-converged replications were discarded.

## 4.5 Bootstrap Sub-Study

Running the BCa bootstrap inside the full factorial is prohibitive
(5,000 replications $\times$ 999 resamples across 192 cells), so we
evaluated it in a focused sub-study targeting the conditions where
its assumption-free construction should matter most. The sub-study
crossed distribution (normal, skewed), $n$ per group (30, 60),
$\rho_{xx}$ (0.60, 0.85), and $\delta$ (0.50, 0.80) under known
reliability, with $R = 1{,}000$ replications per cell and $B = 999$
resamples per replication. On every replicate, the BCa interval —
computed by the package's own bootstrap code — was compared with
the Hunter--Schmidt and Bonett intervals on the same data, so the
three methods are compared pairwise rather than across independent
runs. All 1,000 replications completed in every cell.

## 4.6 Additional Sub-Studies

Four further sub-studies extend the evaluation beyond the main
factorial.

First, the *reliability-uncertainty interval*. In a design crossing
test length ($k = 4$ or $10$ items), $n$ per group (30, 60), and
$\rho_{xx}$ (0.60, 0.85) at $\delta = 0.50$ ($R = 2{,}000$), each
replicate estimated $\alpha$ from the item data and estimated its
standard error by a nonparametric bootstrap over persons
($B = 200$) — the procedure an applied researcher could follow. We
then compared the naive Hunter--Schmidt interval evaluated at
$\hat{\alpha}$ with the interval that additionally propagates
$\widehat{SE}(\hat{\alpha})$ through `rxx_se` (Section 2.3.4).

Second, *design robustness*: (a) unbalanced groups with equal
variances ($n_1 : n_2 = 1{:}3$, $n_1 \in \{30, 60\}$) and (b)
heteroscedastic true scores under balanced groups (true-score
variance ratio 2:1, equal reliability in both groups), each crossed
with $\rho_{xx} \in \{0.60, 0.85\}$ at $\delta = 0.50$
($R = 5{,}000$), comparing Hunter--Schmidt and Bonett. In both
blocks the population effect is defined on the average true-score
standard deviation, which coincides with the pooled standardizer by
construction. The combined case — unbalanced *and* heteroscedastic,
where the pooled-SD estimand itself becomes ambiguous — remains
outside the present scope.

Third, *severe skewness*: the bootstrap comparison of Section 4.5
was repeated with scores generated from a standardized $\chi^2(1)$
distribution (skewness $\approx 2.83$, roughly twice that of the
main design's skewed condition) at $\delta = 0.80$,
$n \in \{30, 60\}$, $\rho_{xx} \in \{0.60, 0.85\}$ ($R = 1{,}000$,
$B = 999$).

Fourth, the *two-sided correction for correlations*: bivariate true
scores with $\rho_{xy} \in \{0.30, 0.50\}$ were observed through two
equally fallible measures ($\rho_{xx} = \rho_{yy} \in \{0.70,
0.85\}$; $n \in \{100, 250\}$; $R = 5{,}000$), and the observed
correlation was corrected with the two-sided Spearman formula of
Section 2.2.
